name: 3M Peltor X4P3E Helmet-Mounted Hearing Protectors
title: 3M Peltor X4P3E Helmet-Mounted Earmuffs
meta: The 3M Peltor X4P3E clips slim earmuffs onto a slotted helmet so hearing protection stays put while you run a saw. Fit, care, and when to replace pads.
tagline: Slim helmet-mounted earmuffs for saw work under a hard hat or climbing helmet.
summary: The 3M Peltor X4P3E is a helmet-mounted version of the slim X4 earmuff, built to clip into the accessory slots on a hard hat or work helmet. It keeps hearing protection on the helmet, so the muffs are there every time the saw starts.
highlights: Helmet-mount version of the Peltor X4 earmuff
P3E attachment clips into standard helmet accessory slots
Cups swing out to a parked position when you do not need them
Slim cup profile works alongside a face screen
Replaceable cushions and foam inserts

body.h: Hearing protection that rides on the helmet
p: Chainsaws, chippers, and stump grinders are loud enough to damage hearing over a normal workday, and the muffs that get left in the truck do nothing. Helmet-mounted earmuffs like the X4P3E solve that by staying attached to the helmet. Flip them down to buck a log, swing them out to talk with the groundie, and they are still there for the next cut.

The P3E arms clip into the side accessory slots found on many hard hats and work helmets. Check that your helmet has compatible slots before you buy, and fit the arms so the cups seal fully around the ears without pressing on the helmet shell. Browse the rest of our hearing protection for headband and plug options.

An earmuff only works if the cushion seals. Hair, glasses arms, and hat brims under the cup all break that seal, so keep the area clear. Wipe sweat and sawdust off the cushions at the end of the day, and replace the cushions and foam inserts when they go hard, flat, or cracked. The Peltor HYX4 hygiene kit is the matching replacement set for X4 cups.
Pick hearing protection with a noise reduction rating suited to the equipment you run, follow 3M's fitting instructions, and pair it with eye and face protection as ANSI Z133 calls for on saw work.

faq.q: Will the X4P3E fit my climbing helmet?
faq.a: It fits helmets with the standard side accessory slots the P3E attachment is made for. Many climbing-style arborist helmets use their own muff mounts, so confirm compatibility with the helmet maker first.

faq.q: What replacement pads does it use?
faq.a: The Peltor HYX4 hygiene kit, which includes new ear cushions and foam inserts for X4 series earmuffs.

name: 3M Peltor HYX4 Earmuff Hygiene Kit
title: Peltor HYX4 Hygiene Kit for X4 Earmuffs
h1: 3M Peltor HYX4 Hygiene Kit for X4 Earmuffs
meta: The Peltor HYX4 hygiene kit replaces worn ear cushions and foam inserts on X4 series earmuffs, so the seal holds and saw noise stays out. When to swap them.
tagline: Fresh cushions and foam inserts to restore the seal on Peltor X4 earmuffs.
summary: The Peltor HYX4 hygiene kit is the replacement cushion and foam insert set for 3M Peltor X4 series earmuffs, including helmet-mounted versions like the X4P3E. Swapping them brings back the seal that sweat, sawdust, and sun slowly take away.
highlights: Replacement ear cushions for Peltor X4 cups
Includes foam inserts for inside the cups
Snaps in without tools
Restores the seal that worn pads lose
Fits headband and helmet-mounted X4 models

p: An earmuff blocks noise with two things: the cup and the seal around your ear. On a tree crew the seal takes the beating. Sweat, bar oil, sawdust, and heat in the truck cab harden the cushions until they no longer conform to the side of your head, and noise leaks straight past them. New cushions are the cheapest way to get back the protection the muff was rated for.

Swap the cushions and foam when they feel stiff, look flattened or cracked, or no longer spring back when pressed. Many crews keep a spare kit in the truck and change pads on a schedule rather than waiting for them to split.

Pull the old cushion off the cup, remove the old foam, set the new foam in place, and press the new cushion on until it seats all the way around. Check that it is fully seated, since a gap at one edge defeats the point. Clean the cups with mild soap and water while they are open, and let them dry before reassembly.
The kit fits X4 series muffs, including the helmet-mounted X4P3E. See our hearing protection section for the earmuffs themselves.

faq.q: How often should I replace earmuff cushions?
faq.a: Replace them whenever they harden, crack, or stop sealing. With daily saw use that is often several times a year. Follow 3M's guidance for your model.

faq.q: Will the HYX4 fit other Peltor earmuffs?
faq.a: It is made for the X4 series. Other Peltor lines use their own kits, so match the kit number to your earmuff model.

name: JBC 36 in. Road Closed Sign
title: JBC 36 in. Road Closed Sign for Tree Work Zones
meta: A 36 inch Road Closed sign for tree crews that shut a street during a removal or crane pick. Where to place it, how to stand it up, and what rules apply.
tagline: A 36 inch Road Closed sign for full street closures on removals and crane jobs.
summary: A 36 inch road closed sign tells drivers well ahead of the work that the street is shut, not just narrowed. Tree crews put it up for removals, crane picks, and chipper setups that take the full roadway.
highlights: 36 in. sign face sized for roadside work zones
Road Closed legend for full closures
Pairs with a sign stand and cones
Easy to load and set up from the truck

body.h: When a tree job closes the road
p: Some jobs cannot be done with a lane shift. A crane parked across the street, a big spar coming down over the road, or a chip truck and loader filling both lanes all mean the road is shut while you work. A Road Closed sign at each end of the work area, backed up with cones or barricades, tells drivers to turn around before they reach the hazard. It is also the sign that keeps a driver from following a GPS route straight into your landing zone.

Set the sign where drivers can see it with time to react and still have a place to turn. Keep it upright, clean, and out of the drop zone, and pick it up as soon as the road reopens so drivers keep trusting your signs.

Closing a public road usually takes a permit and sometimes a police detail. Sign placement and spacing should follow the MUTCD and your state and local rules, and ANSI Z133 expects a work zone plan whenever traffic is affected. Flaggers need training. Two signs and a stack of cones in the truck mean you are ready when a job turns out to need a closure.
A sign stand keeps a 36 inch sign steady in wind. See our traffic control gear for stands, cones, and other work zone signs.

faq.q: Do I need a permit to close a road for tree work?
faq.a: Usually, yes. Check with the city, county, or state agency that owns the road before you plan a closure.

faq.q: Is one sign enough?
faq.a: No. A closure normally needs signs and channelizing devices at each approach, laid out to MUTCD and local requirements.

name: JBC 36 in. Work Area Ahead Sign
title: JBC 36 in. Work Area Ahead Sign for Tree Crews
h1: JBC 36 in. Work Area Ahead Sign
meta: A 36 inch Work Area Ahead sign gives drivers advance warning of a tree crew on the roadside. Where to place it, what it pairs with, and the rules to follow.
tagline: A 36 inch advance warning sign for roadside tree and utility work.
summary: A work area ahead sign is the first thing a driver sees before your trucks, chipper, and ground crew. This 36 inch version is sized for roadside jobs where the crew is working on or near the travel lane.
highlights: 36 in. advance warning sign
Work Area Ahead legend
Sized for roadside work zones
Works with a sign stand, cones, and flaggers

p: Most tree crews spend a lot of time on the shoulder: trimming over a road, dragging brush to the chipper, or parking a bucket truck in a lane. Drivers do not expect people and equipment there. An advance warning sign set well before the work zone buys them the seconds they need to slow down and move over. On fast roads, the sign often needs to go farther out than seems natural, so drivers coming around a bend still have room to brake.

Place the sign so it is visible from a distance, not hidden behind a parked truck or a curve. On a two-way road, cover both approaches. Take it down when the crew leaves, because a warning sign left out with no work behind it teaches drivers to ignore the next one.

body.h: Part of a work zone setup
p: The sign is only the start of the layout. Cones or drums, a lane taper where needed, and trained flaggers finish the job. Follow the MUTCD and local rules for spacing, and plan traffic control as part of the job briefing as ANSI Z133 expects. Keep the sign face clean, since a coat of road grime and sawdust cuts its visibility, especially at dawn and dusk.
Pair it with a sign stand that keeps it upright in wind. Our traffic control section has stands, cones, and other signs.

faq.q: How far ahead should the sign go?
faq.a: It depends on road speed and conditions. Use the MUTCD and your local agency's spacing tables for the road you are working on.

faq.q: Can I use it for a full road closure?
faq.a: Use it as advance warning, but a full closure also needs Road Closed signs and barricades at the closure itself.

name: Plasticade Tree Work Ahead Sign
title: Plasticade Tree Work Ahead Sign for Roadside Jobs
meta: A Plasticade Tree Work Ahead sign tells drivers exactly why the road narrows: a tree crew is on site. Placement tips and how it fits into a work zone setup.
tagline: A plastic Tree Work Ahead warning sign for roadside crews.
summary: A tree work ahead sign does more than a generic warning: it tells drivers there may be falling limbs, brush on the shoulder, and people near the lane. This Plasticade sign is a lightweight plastic option crews can set out and pick up quickly.
highlights: Tree Work Ahead legend tells drivers what to expect
Plastic construction is light to carry
Quick to set out and pick up
Use with cones, stands, and flaggers

body.h: A sign that names the hazard
p: Drivers have learned to tune out generic orange signs. A sign that says tree work gets more attention, because it tells them what is coming: trucks, a chipper, limbs coming down, and people on foot near the lane. That extra bit of attention is what you want while a groundie is feeding brush ten feet from traffic. It also helps the crew: a driver who knows tree work is ahead is less likely to be surprised by a groundie stepping out from behind the chipper.
Set the sign on each approach, far enough out that drivers can slow down before they reach the first truck. Keep it clean and upright, and pull it in when the job wraps up.

Treat the sign as one piece of a layout that also includes cones, a taper if a lane is closed, and trained flaggers when traffic has to stop. Follow the MUTCD and your state rules for spacing, and plan traffic control during the job briefing as ANSI Z133 expects. Plastic signs are light, so a sturdy base or ballast keeps them from tipping over in gusts from passing trucks.
Check the sign before buying if a road authority requires a specific sheeting or size on the roads you work. Browse our traffic control gear for stands and other signs.

faq.q: Is a Tree Work Ahead sign required?
faq.a: Requirements vary by road agency. Many crews use it alongside the standard advance warning signs the MUTCD and local rules call for.

faq.q: Does it need a stand?
faq.a: Use a stand or base suited to the sign so it stays upright in wind and passing traffic.

name: 10.5mm Replacement Rope Bridge with Sewn Eyes
title: 10.5mm Replacement Rope Bridge with Sewn Eyes
h1: 10.5mm Replacement Rope Bridge with Sewn Eyes
meta: A 10.5mm replacement rope bridge with sewn eyes for arborist saddles. How to size it, when to retire the old bridge, and what to check before you climb.
tagline: A sewn-eye rope bridge to replace a worn bridge on your climbing saddle.
summary: A replacement rope bridge is the cheapest way to keep a good saddle in service. This 10.5mm bridge has sewn eyes at each end and is meant to swap in when the bridge on your saddle is worn, glazed, or due for retirement.
highlights: 10.5mm rope bridge
Sewn eyes at both ends
Replaces a worn saddle bridge
Check length and attachment against your saddle

p: On a bridge saddle, the bridge carries your weight and takes the friction of the ring or carabiner sliding back and forth all day. It is usually the first part of the saddle to show wear: fuzzing, glazing, a flat spot where the ring rides, or stiffness from sap and dirt. Replacing it on schedule is cheaper than replacing the saddle and safer than nursing an old bridge along. Keep a log of when the bridge went into service so you know when it is due.

Most saddle makers set a retirement interval for the bridge and expect it to be inspected before every climb. Look for cuts, core damage, heat glazing, contamination, and any damage at the sewn terminations.

Bridges are not universal. Match the length, diameter, and end terminations to what your saddle maker specifies, and install it exactly as their instructions show, including any bridge rings or attachment points. If your saddle calls for a different diameter or length, use that one.

Have a competent person check the setup before you weight it. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard, be used per ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, and be inspected each day. More saddle parts are in this section.

faq.q: Will this bridge fit my saddle?
faq.a: Only if your saddle maker approves a 10.5mm sewn-eye bridge of this length. Check the saddle manual before you order.

faq.q: How often should I replace a saddle bridge?
faq.a: Follow the saddle maker's retirement guidance, and retire it immediately if inspection shows cuts, glazing, core damage, or damaged stitching.

name: 11mm Replacement Rope Bridge, KMIII Max (Black and Yellow)
title: 11mm Replacement Rope Bridge, KMIII Max Black/Yellow
meta: An 11mm replacement rope bridge in black and yellow KMIII Max static rope for arborist saddles. Sizing, inspection, and when to retire the old bridge.
tagline: An 11mm static rope bridge for swapping out a worn saddle bridge.
summary: This 11mm replacement rope bridge is made from KMIII Max static kernmantle rope in black and yellow. Static rope keeps stretch low, so the bridge stays a consistent length as it slides on your ring or carabiner all day.
highlights: 11mm static kernmantle rope
KMIII Max in black and yellow
Low stretch keeps bridge length consistent
Replaces a worn or retired saddle bridge

body.h: A static bridge for a bridge saddle
p: The bridge is the part of your saddle that sees the most friction. Your center ring or carabiner slides on it every time you shift sides, and it carries your weight the whole climb. A tight-weave static kernmantle like KMIII Max resists that abrasion and does not stretch much, so the bridge length you set up on the ground is the length you have in the tree. Bridges see a lot of side-to-side travel on a pruning climb, and a firm static rope holds up to that better than a soft, stretchy one.
The high-visibility black and yellow color also makes wear and dirt easier to see during your pre-climb check.

Saddles take different bridge lengths, diameters, and terminations. Confirm that an 11mm bridge of this length and end style is approved by your saddle's maker, then install it exactly as the saddle manual shows. Do not tie your own improvised replacement.

Inspect the bridge before every climb for cuts, glazing, flat spots, contamination, and damaged ends, and retire it on the maker's schedule. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard and be used per ANSI Z133 and manufacturer instructions by trained climbers. Other saddle parts are listed here.

faq.q: Is KMIII Max a static rope?
faq.a: Yes. It is a low-stretch kernmantle rope, which suits a saddle bridge that should hold its length.

faq.q: Can I use an 11mm bridge on a saddle that came with a thinner one?
faq.a: Only if the saddle maker approves it. Diameter affects how rings and hardware fit and run, so check the manual first.

name: 2 in. Ring-to-Ring Friction Saver
title: 2 in. Ring-to-Ring Friction Saver for Tree Climbing
meta: A ring-to-ring friction saver with 2 inch rings protects bark and your climbing line at the tie-in point and lets you retrieve it from the ground. How it works.
tagline: A simple ring-to-ring friction saver for a cleaner tie-in and less rope wear.
summary: A ring-to-ring friction saver puts two metal rings at your tie-in point so the climbing line runs on metal instead of bark. This version uses 2 inch rings, large enough to pass a knot or hitch through when you retrieve it from the ground.
highlights: Two 2 in. rings, one small and one large in most designs
Protects cambium at the tie-in crotch
Reduces rope wear and friction for moving rope climbing
Retrievable from the ground with the right technique

p: When you climb on a moving rope system, the line slides over the tie-in crotch every time you advance or descend. That friction heats the rope, glazes the bark, and can damage the cambium on the tree you are being paid to care for. A ring-to-ring friction saver wraps the limb and gives the rope a smooth pair of rings to run through instead. Because the rope runs through metal rings, it also tends to run with less wear than it would over rough bark, so your climbing line lasts longer.
Less friction also means easier advancing of your hitch and smoother descents, which adds up over a full day of pruning.

Choose a sound limb of adequate size, set the saver so the rings sit at the top of the crotch, and make sure the rings cannot be pulled through each other in your setup. Learn the retrieval method from a qualified trainer before relying on it, since the knot and ring order matter.

Inspect the rings for grooves and the sling for cuts, glazing, and abrasion before each climb. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard and be used per ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions. Compare other friction savers here.

faq.q: Can I retrieve a ring-to-ring friction saver from the ground?
faq.a: Yes, with the correct retrieval setup. Practice it low with a trainer before you depend on it at height.

faq.q: Does it work for SRS climbing?
faq.a: It is built for moving rope systems. For a stationary rope system, use an anchor method suited to SRS.

name: 3/4 in. Soft Anchor Rigging Sling with Tylaska Large Basilisk
title: 3/4 in. Soft Anchor Rigging Sling with Tylaska Basilisk
h1: 3/4 in. Soft Anchor Rigging Sling with Tylaska Large Basilisk
meta: A 3/4 inch soft anchor rigging sling fitted with a Tylaska Large Basilisk for setting heavy rigging points on removals. Uses, setup, and inspection.
tagline: A heavy rope rigging sling with Tylaska hardware for big rigging points.
summary: A soft anchor rigging sling gives you a rope-based rigging point you can set around a stem or limb without a steel shackle. This 3/4 inch version is fitted with a Tylaska Large Basilisk and is meant for heavier rigging on removals.
highlights: 3/4 in. rope sling for heavy rigging
Fitted with a Tylaska Large Basilisk
Soft on bark compared with chain or wire
Light to carry aloft
Read the working load before every rig

body.h: A soft rigging point for big wood
p: Heavy removals need a rigging point that can take shock loads from big pieces. A rope sling is lighter than chain, easier to carry up the tree, and kinder to the stem. At 3/4 inch, this sling sits at the heavy end for climber-carried rigging, for setting a block or anchoring a lowering line on large spars.

The Tylaska Large Basilisk on this sling is marine-grade hardware from a maker known for high-strength sailing fittings. Read the hardware and sling documentation to understand how this assembly is meant to be set and loaded before taking it aloft.

Rigging loads are often several times the weight of the piece once it starts to fall. Know the rated working load of the whole assembly and stay within it, set the sling on sound wood, and keep it away from the saw. Avoid sharp edges and pad where needed.

Inspect the rope for cuts, glazing, pulled strands, and core damage, and check the Tylaska fitting for cracks, deformation, and wear before each job. Rigging must follow ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions and be run by trained people. More rigging slings are in this section.

faq.q: What is the difference between the 3/4 in. and 5/8 in. versions?
faq.a: The 3/4 in. sling is the heavier, stronger option and uses the Large Basilisk. The 5/8 in. sling is lighter for mid-size rigging. Check each tag for ratings.

faq.q: Can I use it to anchor a lowering line?
faq.a: Yes, a soft anchor sling is commonly used to set a rigging point for a block or lowering setup, within its rated working load.

name: 4 ft. Endless Loop Polyester Round Sling
title: 4 ft. Endless Loop Polyester Round Sling
h1: 4 ft. Endless Loop Polyester Round Sling
meta: A 4 ft endless loop polyester round sling for crane picks, rigging points, and log lifts on tree jobs. How to hitch it, read the tag, and inspect it.
tagline: A short polyester round sling for crane picks and rigging points.
summary: A 4 ft endless loop polyester round sling is a short, soft sling for choking smaller stems, setting rigging points, and lifting logs at the landing. It has no eyes or hardware, so it lies flat against the wood and comes free easily.
highlights: Endless loop, no eyes to wear
Polyester core yarns in a protective cover
4 ft. length for smaller stems and tight spots
Choker, basket, and vertical hitches
Capacity printed on the tag
specs: On sling tag; vary by hitch

body.h: Where a short round sling earns its place
p: Long slings get all the attention on crane jobs, but a 4 ft round sling is the one you reach for on smaller stems, limbs, and logs. Choked around a leader it makes a quick pick point. Doubled around a log at the landing it lets the loader or crane lift it without scarring. It also makes a tidy rigging point for a block on a modest limb. Keep a couple in the truck for odd jobs like lifting a log onto a trailer.
Because it is soft and has no hardware, it will not chew bark, and it is easy to hand up to a climber or clip to the boom.

body.h: Read the tag, inspect every lift
p: Every round sling carries a tag with its rated capacity for vertical, choker, and basket hitches. The choker rating is lower, and basket capacity drops as leg angles widen. If the tag is missing or unreadable, take the sling out of service.

Look for cuts, burns, melted spots, exposed core yarns, and damaged stitching before each use, and keep the sling away from the chain. Crane and rigging work should follow ANSI Z133, the sling maker's instructions, and a qualified operator. See all crane slings for longer sizes.

faq.q: Is 4 ft. the loop length or the cut length?
faq.a: Round slings are typically sized by bearing-point-to-bearing-point length when laid flat. Check the sling tag for the exact length and ratings.

faq.q: Can I tie a knot in a round sling?
faq.a: No. Knots reduce strength and damage the core. Use the hitches the tag rates.

name: 5/16 in. Soft Shackle
title: 5/16 in. Soft Shackle for Arborist Rigging
meta: A 5/16 inch soft shackle is a light rope connector for rigging blocks, rings, and slings on tree jobs. How it closes, where it fits, and how to inspect it.
tagline: A light rope connector that replaces a steel shackle in many rigging setups.
summary: A 5/16 soft shackle is a rope connector closed with a stopper knot and loop instead of a pin. It does many jobs a small steel shackle does, connecting blocks, rings, and slings, at a fraction of the weight and without metal to damage bark.
highlights: 5/16 in. rope soft shackle
Closes with a stopper knot and loop, no pin to lose
Much lighter than a comparable steel shackle
Will not scar bark or other hardware
Inspect like any rope rigging component

p: Soft shackles started in sailing and found a home in tree rigging because they are light, strong for their weight, and easy to use with gloves on. Use one to connect a rigging block to a sling, join a ring to a loop, or close a soft anchor around a stem. There is no pin to drop from the tree and no steel to bang against your other hardware. They also pack small, so a few can ride on your saddle or in the rigging bag without adding much weight.
At 5/16 inch, this size suits light to moderate rigging and accessory connections. For heavy removals, step up to a larger shackle or steel hardware rated for the load.

Open the shackle, pass the loop around what you are connecting, push the stopper knot through the loop, and tighten it until the knot seats firmly. A soft shackle that is not fully seated can open under load, so check it every time.

Know the rated working load and stay within it. Inspect for cuts, glazing, pulled strands, and wear at the knot and loop, and retire it if in doubt. Follow ANSI Z133 and the maker's instructions for all rigging. See other rings and rigging hardware here.

faq.q: Can a soft shackle replace a steel shackle?
faq.a: In many rigging connections, yes, as long as its rated load suits the job and it is protected from sharp edges and the saw.

faq.q: Is a soft shackle life-support gear?
faq.a: Use it for rigging unless the maker specifically rates and approves it for climbing.

name: 5/8 in. Soft Anchor Rigging Sling with Tylaska Basilisk
title: 5/8 in. Soft Anchor Rigging Sling with Tylaska Basilisk
h1: 5/8 in. Soft Anchor Rigging Sling with Tylaska Basilisk
meta: A 5/8 inch soft anchor rigging sling with a Tylaska Basilisk for setting rigging points on everyday removals. Where it fits, setup notes, and inspection.
tagline: A mid-size rope rigging sling with Tylaska hardware for everyday removals.
summary: The 5/8 soft anchor rigging sling is a rope rigging point fitted with a Tylaska Basilisk. It sits in the middle of the range: strong enough for regular removal rigging, light enough to carry up without a fight.
highlights: 5/8 in. rope sling
Fitted with a Tylaska Basilisk
Lighter than chain or steel-heavy setups
Gentle on bark
Check rated working load before rigging

p: Most removals are not crane jobs. They are a climber, a block, a lowering line, and a groundie running a lowering device. For that work a 5/8 inch soft anchor sling is a practical size: set it around the stem above the work, hang the block, and you have a rigging point that weighs little and does not chew up the tree. It also works well as a natural crotch alternative when the tree does not offer a clean spot to rig over.
The Tylaska Basilisk fitted to the sling is high-strength marine hardware. Read the sling and hardware documentation for how the assembly is meant to be set and loaded before you use it aloft.

Dynamic loads in rigging can be much larger than the static weight of the piece. Know the working load of the whole sling and hardware assembly and stay inside it, use sound wood, and keep the sling out of the kerf.

Check the rope for cuts, glazing, and core damage, and the Tylaska fitting for cracks or wear, before each job. Rigging must follow ANSI Z133 and manufacturer instructions and be done by trained crews. Compare other rigging slings here, including the 3/4 inch version for heavier wood.

faq.q: When should I choose the 3/4 in. version instead?
faq.a: When pieces are larger and loads higher. Compare the rated working loads on each sling against the rigging you plan.

faq.q: Can I choke it around a stem?
faq.a: Set it as the maker's instructions describe for this assembly, on sound wood and within its rated load.

name: Husqvarna 3/16 in. Chainsaw Files (2-Pack)
title: Husqvarna 3/16 Chainsaw Files (2-Pack)
meta: Husqvarna 3/16 chainsaw files, round, two per pack, for sharpening chains that call for a 4.8mm file. Which chains they fit and how to file well.
tagline: Two 3/16 in. round files for touching up chain on the job.
summary: The Husqvarna 3/16 chainsaw file is a round file for sharpening chain that calls for a 3/16 inch (4.8mm) file, which includes many .325 pitch chains. The two-pack lets you keep one in the truck and one in the saw kit.
highlights: 3/16 in. (4.8mm) round file
Two files per pack
Common size for many .325 pitch chains
Fits standard file handles and guides

body.h: Match the file to the chain
p: The right file diameter is the one your chain maker specifies, and it is printed on the chain box or in the saw manual. A 3/16 inch file is the usual size for many .325 pitch chains found on mid-size saws. Too small and you hook the cutter; too large and you round off the top plate. Two files in the pack means one stays sharp while the other is in use.
Sharp chain matters on a tree job. A dull saw makes you push, throws dust instead of chips, and wanders in the cut, which makes hinges harder to control and wears out the climber.

Use a handle and a file guide to hold the correct angle and depth, and file from the inside of the cutter outward with even strokes. Give every cutter the same number of strokes so they stay the same length, then check the depth gauges. Rotate the file a little as you go so it wears evenly, and replace it once it stops biting. Brush filings and sawdust off the file with a file card or stiff brush so the teeth keep cutting, and store files where they will not rattle against other steel.
Wear gloves and lock the bar in a vise or stump vise. See our wrenches and files for handles, guides, and flat files.

faq.q: What chains use a 3/16 in. file?
faq.a: Many .325 pitch chains do, but check the file size printed on your chain box or in the saw manual.

faq.q: Do these come with a handle?
faq.a: Handles are usually sold separately. A handle gives better control and protects your hand.

name: Husqvarna 5/32 in. Chainsaw Files (2-Pack)
title: Husqvarna 5/32 Chainsaw Files (2-Pack)
meta: Husqvarna 5/32 chainsaw files, round, two per pack, for chains that call for a 4.0mm file such as many 3/8 low-profile chains. Fit and filing tips.
tagline: Two 5/32 in. round files for small-pitch chain on top-handle and light saws.
summary: The Husqvarna 5/32 chainsaw file is a 4.0mm round file for sharpening small-pitch chain, including many 3/8 low-profile chains used on top-handle saws and light pruning saws. Two files come in the pack.
highlights: 5/32 in. (4.0mm) round file
Two files per pack
Common size for many 3/8 low-profile chains
Good fit for top-handle saw maintenance

body.h: The file for your top-handle chain
p: Most climbers' top-handle saws run small-pitch chain, and a lot of that chain calls for a 5/32 inch file. A top-handle with dull chain is a real problem aloft: you push harder, the saw bucks, and one-handed control gets worse. Keeping a fresh 5/32 file in the climbing kit means a quick touch-up on the lunch break. Many climbers keep the second file in the truck so a worn one never holds up the job.
Always confirm the file size printed on the chain box or in the saw manual, since some small chains call for a different diameter.

Use a file handle and guide to hold angle and depth, file from the inside of each cutter out, and keep strokes even so the cutters stay matched. After a few sharpenings, check and lower the depth gauges with a flat file and gauge tool. A round file that skates instead of cutting is worn out and should be replaced. Brush filings and sawdust off the file with a file card or stiff brush so the teeth keep cutting, and store files where they will not rattle against other steel.
Clamp the bar so the saw cannot move, and wear gloves. See our wrenches and files for handles, guides, and depth gauge files.

faq.q: Which chains use a 5/32 in. file?
faq.a: Many 3/8 low-profile and 1/4 in. pitch chains do. Check the file size on your chain box or in the saw manual.

faq.q: How long does a round file last?
faq.a: It depends on how often you file and how hard you press. Replace it when it stops cutting cleanly.

name: DMM Kwiklock Modified D Steel Carabiner
title: DMM Kwiklock Modified D Steel Carabiner
h1: DMM Kwiklock Modified D Steel Carabiner
meta: A Kwiklock modified D steel carabiner with an auto-locking gate for heavy-wear spots on an arborist setup. Where steel makes sense and how to inspect it.
tagline: A steel auto-locking modified D for spots where aluminum wears out fast.
summary: The Kwiklock modified D steel carabiner pairs a tough steel body with an auto-locking gate. Steel resists the grooving that rope and rings wear into aluminum, so it suits high-wear spots like a friction saver, rigging, or a lanyard end.
highlights: Steel body resists rope and ring wear
Modified D shape keeps loads near the spine
Kwiklock auto-locking gate
Heavier than aluminum but longer-lasting in wear spots
Check markings for strength and certification

p: Aluminum carabiners are light, which is why most climbers carry them. The trade-off is wear: a moving rope, a running ring, or grit on the line slowly cuts a groove into aluminum. Steel holds up far longer in those spots. Climbers use steel carabiners where something runs through them all day, such as a friction saver or rigging, and accept the extra weight in return. Steel is also more forgiving of the knocks and drops that come with rigging work.
The modified D shape keeps the load close to the spine, which is the strongest part of the carabiner, while still opening wide enough to clip a ring or rope.

An auto-locking gate closes and locks on its own when released, which is what most standards and training programs expect for life-support connections. Check that the gate closes and locks fully every time, and keep it clean of sap and grit.

Read the strength and certification markings on the spine to confirm it suits your use. Inspect for grooves, cracks, corrosion, and gate problems before each climb, and retire it if anything looks off. Use per ANSI Z133 and the maker's instructions. Compare other auto-locking carabiners here.

faq.q: Is a steel carabiner OK for climbing?
faq.a: Yes, if it is rated and certified for life support and used as the maker directs. Check the markings on the spine.

faq.q: Why choose steel if it is heavier?
faq.a: Steel wears far more slowly in spots where rope or hardware runs through the carabiner all day.

name: Petzl Microflip Wire Core Replacement Lanyard
title: Petzl Microflip Replacement Lanyard, Wire Core
h1: Petzl Microflip Replacement Lanyard, Wire Core
meta: The Petzl Microflip replacement lanyard puts a new steel-core flipline into your Microflip adjuster. Available lengths, fit, and when it is time to replace it.
tagline: A replacement steel-core lanyard rope for the Petzl Microflip adjuster.
summary: The Petzl Microflip replacement lanyard is the steel-core rope for the Microflip adjustable lanyard. It lets you keep your adjuster in service and replace only the lanyard rope when it wears out.
highlights: Steel wire core resists accidental saw contact
Made for the Petzl Microflip adjuster
Offered in several lengths
Replace the rope, keep the adjuster
Inspect before every climb

p: Spur climbers on removals spend the day with a saw running close to their flipline. A wire core lanyard has a steel cable inside the rope, which gives far more resistance to an accidental touch from the chain than an all-fiber line. It is not saw-proof, but it buys margin where it matters most. Keep the saw on the opposite side of the lanyard when you can, and slow down near the rope.
The Microflip adjuster lets you lengthen and shorten the lanyard one-handed while staying positioned on the stem. This replacement lanyard lets you renew the worn rope without buying a whole new kit.

Pick a length that wraps the largest stems you climb with enough tail left to work. Longer lanyards cover big trunks but add weight and loose rope. Install it exactly as Petzl's instructions describe, and check that the adjuster grips and releases properly before you trust it at height.

Retire a lanyard with any cut through the sheath, exposed or kinked wire, crushing, or heat damage. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard, be used per ANSI Z133 and Petzl's instructions, and be inspected by a trained climber. See other fliplines and lanyards here.

faq.q: Will this lanyard fit a non-Petzl adjuster?
faq.a: It is made for the Petzl Microflip. Use it only with adjusters Petzl approves for it.

faq.q: Is a wire core lanyard cut-proof?
faq.a: No. The steel core improves resistance to accidental saw contact, but any lanyard can be cut. Keep the saw clear.

name: Pferd Stump Vise
title: Pferd Stump Vise for Sharpening Chain in the Field
meta: The Pferd stump vise drives into a stump or log and clamps your chainsaw bar so you can file chain on the job site. How to set it up and file safely.
tagline: A portable vise that clamps your bar to a stump for field sharpening.
summary: The Pferd stump vise is a portable bar clamp you tap into a stump or round, then tighten onto your chainsaw bar. It holds the saw steady so you can sharpen chain properly in the field instead of balancing it on the tailgate.
highlights: Tap into a stump or log, clamp the bar
Holds the saw steady for even filing
Small enough to live in the saw kit
Works with round and flat files and guides
specs: Holding the bar for field sharpening

body.h: Sharpen on site, not in the shop
p: Chain dulls fast on a tree job. Grit in the bark, a nicked rock at the base, or a few hours of bucking all take the edge off. The quickest fix is a touch-up right where you are working, and the stump vise makes that practical. Tap it into a fresh stump or a round, set the bar in the jaws, tighten, and the saw sits steady while you file. It is also handy for quick bar dressing and chain checks at lunch.
A steady bar means consistent angles and even cutter lengths, which gives you a chain that cuts straight. Balancing the saw on your knee or the tailgate rarely gets you there.

Drive the vise into solid wood, not punky stump, so it does not wobble. Clamp the bar near the middle with enough chain exposed to file, and rotate the chain around as you work. Keep the chain brake on and the engine off while filing, and wear gloves. Pull it out of the stump when you leave so it does not end up in the chipper.
Pair it with the right round file for your chain and a flat file for depth gauges. Our wrenches and files section has both.

faq.q: Does the stump vise work on any bar?
faq.a: It clamps the bar body, so it suits common bar sizes. Very wide or very small bars may fit less securely.

faq.q: Can I use it on a log instead of a stump?
faq.a: Yes. Any solid round or log end you can drive it into will work.

name: The Splice Shop Deluxe Bullet Throw Weight
title: The Splice Shop Deluxe Bullet Throw Weight
h1: The Splice Shop Deluxe Bullet Throw Weight
meta: The Splice Shop Deluxe Bullet throw weight is a bullet-shaped throw bag for setting throw line through tight canopy. How it compares and how to throw safely.
tagline: A bullet-shaped throw weight that slips through tight branch unions.
summary: The Splice Shop Deluxe Bullet throw weight is a narrow, bullet-shaped throw bag made to slip through tight crotches and clutter that catch a round bag. Clip it to your throw line and use it to set climbing and rigging lines from the ground.
highlights: Bullet shape slides through tight unions
Less likely to hang up on small twigs
Attachment ring for throw line
Use with a throw line cube or bag

p: A round throw bag works fine in open canopy, but in dense crowns it catches every small twig and wedges in narrow unions. A bullet-shaped weight leads with a narrow nose, so it slips through clutter and drops more cleanly on the far side of the limb. That means fewer re-throws and fewer bags stuck in the tree. A good throw weight is one of the cheapest ways to speed up the start of every climb.
Most climbers carry more than one weight size. Lighter bags for low shots and thin line, heavier ones for high shots and when you need the bag to pull line back down.

Clear the drop zone before every throw and call out so the crew knows a weight is coming down. Watch for power lines, which are a serious hazard for throw lines and climbing lines alike. Never stand under the weight as it falls back. If a weight hangs up, do not yank hard on thin line; work it free or pull it down with care.
Inspect the bag and attachment ring for wear and replace a damaged bag before it lets go mid-throw. Browse the rest of our throw weights and line for line, cubes, and kits.

faq.q: What throw line works with it?
faq.a: Standard arborist throw lines in common diameters. Match the bag weight to the line and the height you are throwing.

faq.q: Is a bullet weight better than a round bag?
faq.a: In tight or cluttered canopy it often is. In open trees either works, so many climbers carry both.

name: Courant Pelican Throw Line Bag
title: Courant Pelican Throw Line Bag for Tangle-Free Line
meta: The Courant Pelican throw line bag stores throw line and weights so they deploy without tangles on the next shot. Why a line bag helps and how to pack it.
tagline: A dedicated throw line bag that keeps line ready to run on the next throw.
summary: The Courant Pelican throw line bag gives your throw line and weights a home that lets the line feed out cleanly on each shot. Line stuffed loose into the bottom of a gear bag tangles; line flaked into a dedicated bag runs.
highlights: Dedicated storage for throw line and weights
Lets line feed out cleanly while throwing
Keeps line off the ground and out of debris
Packs into the truck or gear bag

p: Setting a line is often the slowest part of starting a climb, and most of that time is spent untangling throw line. Thin, slick line coils, kinks, and grabs sticks and leaves the moment it touches the ground. A throw line bag gives the line somewhere clean to sit, open-mouthed, so it feeds out freely when the weight goes up. It also keeps line clean, which matters because grit and sap make throw line stiff and slow.
Courant designs gear for working climbers, and a dedicated bag like the Pelican is one of those small items that saves a few minutes on every tree.

Feed the line into the bag loosely by hand rather than coiling it, so it pays out without twists. Keep the bag open and upright near your feet while throwing, and keep the weight clear of the line so it does not snag on the way out. Some climbers keep a spare weight clipped in the bag so they can switch sizes without walking back to the truck.
Shake out sawdust and twigs now and then, and check the line for fuzzing or damage as you pack it. Our throw weight and line section has line, weights, and kits to go with it.

faq.q: Should I coil throw line into the bag?
faq.a: No. Stuff it loosely by hand. Coiling adds twists that turn into tangles when you throw.

faq.q: Will it hold more than one throw line?
faq.a: Keep one line per bag or compartment so they do not tangle with each other.

name: Weaver WLC-760 Arborist Saddle
title: Weaver WLC-760 Arborist Saddle: Fit and Features
meta: The Weaver WLC-760 arborist saddle is a work positioning saddle for tree climbers. What to check for fit and comfort, plus inspection and retirement tips.
tagline: A Weaver work positioning saddle for tree climbers.
summary: The Weaver WLC-760 saddle is a work positioning saddle from Weaver Leather, a long-time maker of tree climbing and utility gear. It is built for climbers who want a supportive saddle with room for the tools a working day needs.
highlights: Weaver work positioning saddle
Side D-rings for lanyard and positioning
Gear loops for saws and tools
Padded back for long days in the tree

p: The saddle is where you spend your day, so fit matters more than any feature list. It should sit snug on the hips without pinching, support your back when you lean into the lanyard, and keep tools where you can reach them without twisting. Weaver saddles have long been a common choice on crews, especially for climbers who spend a lot of time on spurs. Think about the work you do most: spur removals reward a firm, supportive saddle, while long pruning climbs reward freedom of movement.
Try on your size with the leg straps adjusted, hang in it if you can, and check that the attachment points line up with the way you climb.

Check webbing, stitching, padding, buckles, and D-rings before every climb. Look for cuts, abrasion, chemical or heat damage, cracked hardware, and pulled stitches, and retire the saddle if any load-bearing part is damaged. Store it clean and dry out of the sun. Keep a record of the saddle's in-service date so you can track its age against Weaver's retirement guidance.
Saddles are life-support gear and must meet the applicable standard and be used per ANSI Z133 and Weaver's instructions by trained climbers. Compare other Weaver saddles here.

faq.q: How do I pick my size?
faq.a: Use Weaver's size chart for your waist and leg measurements, and try it on with the clothing you climb in.

faq.q: How long does a saddle last?
faq.a: It depends on use and care. Follow Weaver's guidance and retire it whenever inspection finds damage to load-bearing parts.

name: Pferd 8 in. Depth Gauge File
title: Pferd 8 in. Depth Gauge File for Chainsaw Chain
meta: The Pferd 8 inch depth gauge file is a flat file for lowering chainsaw rakers so a sharp chain keeps biting. When to file depth gauges and how to do it.
tagline: An 8 in. flat file for keeping chain depth gauges at the right height.
summary: The Pferd depth gauge file is an 8 inch flat file for taking down the depth gauges, or rakers, on chainsaw chain. Sharp cutters only help if the gauges in front of them let the chain take a proper bite.
highlights: 8 in. flat file
For lowering chain depth gauges
Use with a depth gauge tool
Fits a standard file handle

p: Each cutter on a chain has a depth gauge in front of it that sets how deep the cutter can bite. Every time you round-file the cutters they get a little lower, and the gauges stay put. After a few sharpenings the chain stops taking a full bite and just skates, even though the cutters are sharp. Taking the gauges down with a flat file brings the cut back. A quality flat file takes metal off in a few controlled strokes.

Leave them too high and the saw cuts slowly; take them too low and the chain grabs and is more prone to kickback. Getting them right matters on every saw, and most of all on a top-handle used one-handed aloft.

Set a depth gauge tool over the chain, file each gauge flush with the tool using a few even strokes, then round off the front of the gauge to keep its original shape. Use the setting your chain maker specifies. Check the gauges every few sharpenings, not every time.
Fit a handle to the file, clamp the bar, and wear gloves. See our wrenches and files for depth gauge tools and handles.

faq.q: How often should I file depth gauges?
faq.a: Check them every few round-file sharpenings and lower them when they stand above the depth gauge tool.

faq.q: Does this file need a handle?
faq.a: A handle is strongly recommended for control and to protect your hand from the file tang.

name: Pferd Wooden File Handle
title: Pferd Wooden File Handle for Chainsaw Files
meta: The Pferd wooden file handle fits onto round and flat chainsaw files for better control and a safer grip while sharpening. How to fit it and keep it tight.
tagline: A simple wooden handle that makes chain filing safer and more accurate.
summary: The Pferd wooden file handle fits onto the tang of a round or flat chainsaw file so you can hold it firmly and file at a steady angle. It is a cheap part that makes a real difference to how well you sharpen.
highlights: Wooden handle for chainsaw files
Covers the sharp file tang
Improves grip and control
Fits round and flat files

p: A file without a handle leaves the tang pointing straight at your palm, and it is hard to hold steady. A handle covers the tang and gives you a full grip, so you can push the file with even pressure and hold the angle across every cutter. Better control means more even cutters, a straighter cutting chain, and fewer filing-related cuts. Wood is light and warm in the hand on a cold morning, and it gives a secure grip even with gloves on.
Many sawyers keep a handle on each file in their kit so they are not swapping one handle between round and flat files.

Push the file tang into the handle and tap the end of the handle on a solid surface to seat it. Do not hammer on the file itself, as files are hard and can chip. If the handle loosens over time, re-seat it, and replace it if the wood splits. Some sawyers mark each handle with the file size so the right file is easy to grab from the kit. A file with a loose or missing handle should not be used until it is fixed.
Find files, guides, and stump vises in our wrenches and files section.

faq.q: Will it fit both round and flat files?
faq.a: It fits standard tanged files. Very large or very small tangs may fit less snugly.

faq.q: How do I remove it from a worn file?
faq.a: Hold the handle and tap the file's edge near the handle against a bench edge to work it loose, keeping hands clear of the file teeth.
